Bessemer Predicts: Robotics and physical AI
Six investor predictions on the state of robotics research and the commercialization of the physical AI ecosystem—plus founders' candid takes on what's evolving in the market in 2026.
No human actually wants to do highly repetitive physical tasks or endure unsafe working conditions in factories or hazardous sites. That observation sounds simple, but the implications are not. Demographic trends across the US, Europe, Japan, and China are building structural, lasting demand for robotics solutions—demand that persists independent of any single technology cycle. Some analysts have projected the robotics market will reach
$38 billion by 2035
— Jeremy Levine, Partner at Bessemer Venture Partners
At Bessemer, we often invest in new categories when we see the intersection of three forces: talent migration, technology breakthroughs, and structural tailwinds. In robotics and physical AI, all three are accelerating simultaneously. Already, we’ve invested in breakthrough teams, as our portfolio spans software, full systems, and foundation models:
Waymo
Robotics predictions for 2026
At a glance: Six predictions for robotics and physical AI in 2026
We're in the GPT-2.5 moment for robotics. Capabilities are real, but the gap between lab performance and field deployment remains wide.
Robotics data is orders of magnitude scarcer than internet text — and closing that gap requires capital at a scale that will quickly separate the well-funded from the rest.
The LLM era had a foundational advantage that robotics does not: the internet. Language models bootstrapped on hundreds of trillions of tokens of freely available text. There is no equivalent corpus for physical AI. Total global robot manipulation data is estimated at roughly 300,000 hours—compared to approximately 1 billion hours of internet video and 300 trillion tokens of text. The gap isn’t incremental; It’s structural.
The cost consequence is direct. Bessemer estimates aggregate robotic data costs across the industry will exceed $3 billion over the next two years, spanning teleoperation, egocentric video, simulation, and physical demonstration collection. Robot data cannot be scraped or purchased from a broker. It has to be generated, task by task, environment by environment. The teams that close this gap fastest will be the ones with the capital to sustain that effort—the same dynamic that gave Waymo and Tesla structural advantages in autonomous driving, where data moats were built on miles and edge cases, not just algorithms.
world models
—neural networks trained on internet-scale video that learn physics through observation. The results are promising: Meta's V-JEPA 2, trained on over a million hours of internet video, achieved 80% zero-shot pick-and-place success on real robot arms with just 62 hours of additional robot-specific data. But world models are themselves expensive to train—NVIDIA's Cosmos required 10,000 H100 GPUs over three months. This is not a free shortcut. It is a capital-intensive bet that physics learned from video generalizes to physical manipulation. The early results are encouraging; full generalization remains unproven.
The second path is simulation and reinforcement learning. Sim-to-real transfer works well for locomotion, but manipulation is harder. How a robot hand interacts with a soft object, how fabric slides between fingers, how liquids behave — these require a fidelity that current simulators don't achieve. Sim-to-real for manipulation is an open research problem, not a solved one.
Prediction 3: Talent concentration will crown winners fast—this is not a market where 50 companies win
Among US robotics companies founded in the last five years that have raised $30M or more, 43% of founders hold PhDs. Nearly half (48%) come from just four institutions: Stanford, MIT, Berkeley, and Carnegie Mellon University. 56% of these companies have at least one PhD co-founder, and 43% came directly from academia. Robotics doesn’t have a broad-based talent ecosystem. It’s a narrow pipeline producing a small number of exceptionally capable people, and those people are already choosing sides.
The talent moat in robotics will compound into winner-takes-most dynamics faster than most people expect. Talent not only attracts more talent, but also capital, which then attracts data partnerships, customer relationships, and the infrastructure to generate proprietary datasets. Each advantage compounds the next.
The teams with the deepest expertise in sim-to-real transfer, manipulation, locomotion, and sensor fusion are building advantages that open-source releases don't easily replicate.
Team composition is the first investment decision in robotics, and it compounds faster here than almost anywhere else. This isn't a market where a long tail of moderately capable companies finds niches and survives. Capital and talent will concentrate quickly. Given how concentrated talent is, and how early the generalized models remain, where does value actually accrue in the stack?
Prediction 4: Full-stack players will capture near-term value— pure-play foundation model companies will need to wait
Unlike the LLM era, where horizontal foundation model companies captured outsized value early, robotics foundation models aren't yet general enough to work out of the box—giving vertically integrated players a meaningful head start.
In software, the API changed everything. Once GPT-4 was callable via a single endpoint, a two-person team could build a product with frontier AI capability on day one. The stack separated cleanly, and quickly. Robotics doesn't work that way yet. Humanoid Robot Safety Standards 2026: Best Compliance Guide
Humanoid robot safety in 2026 is governed by ISO 10218:2025, ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025, and developing ISO 25785-1. Covers fall zones, battery protocols, OSHA compliance, and risk assessment matrix.
Ulrich Baldauf
Key Takeaways
Humanoid robot safety in 2026 is governed by ISO 10218:2025 and ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025, with ISO 25785-1 under development specifically for dynamically stable robots.
Certification now covers applications, not just hardware
Your facility bought a “collaborative” humanoid robot. The vendor said it’s safe. Six months later, OSHA cites you for an unsafe application. The robot hasn’t changed. Your deployment failed compliance.
Traditional collaborative robot rules don’t cover walking machines. ISO/TS 15066 addressed contact forces for stationary arms. Humanoid robots walk, balance, and carry energy-dense batteries. Different risks need different standards. Understanding
how humanoid robots work
, from locomotion to battery systems, makes those risk differences concrete.
This humanoid robot safety guide explains the current regulatory framework and emerging standards. You’ll learn how
ISO 10218-1:2025
shifted from hardware to application certification. You’ll understand the developing ISO 25785-1 requirements for dynamic stability. You’ll see how OSHA applies existing rules to walking robots. Learn more
about my methodology
instead.
The 2025 update to ISO 10218-1 shifts humanoid robot safety focus from hardware definitions to collaborative application certification. According to
IDEC USA analysis
, ISO 10218-2:2025 nearly tripled in length, with the safety requirements section growing from 28 to 50 pages, reflecting the scope of regulatory expansion. The revision involved experts from more than 20 countries over eight years. Buying a robot with force-limiting joints no longer guarantees compliance.
The term “collaborative robot” implied the machine itself was inherently safe. A robot arm that stopped on contact met the definition. Regulators now recognize that safety depends on the entire system. The robot, the task, the workspace, and the human workflow all contribute to risk.
Need Documentation Templates for Your Deployment?
The Robot Safety Documentation Toolkit 2026 includes pre-populated risk assessment templates, a humanoid-specific LOTO procedure, and facility readiness checklists aligned with ISO 10218:2025 and EU MR 2023/1230.
View the Toolkit ($397)
ISO 25785-1
, currently under development, will establish safety requirements for dynamically stable robots, machines that require active balance control to remain upright. Traditional robot arms bolt to the floor. Humanoid robots walk. Walking introduces fall risk.
Diagram:
Important:
As of January 2026, ISO 25785-1 remains a Working Draft. The ISO working group, led by experts from Agility Robotics, Boston Dynamics, and the A3 Association, held its most recent session in Barcelona in October 2025. Final publication is expected in 2026 or 2027. Until then, facilities should apply its principles as best-practice guidance while relying on ISO 10218 and manufacturer specifications for compliance.
In contrast, a stationary arm in a known position presents predictable hazards. A walking robot that loses power tips over. The direction and distance of the fall depend on speed, load, and floor angle. ISO 25785-1 aims to quantify that variability, filling the most critical humanoid robot safety gap in current standards.
“Active Balance Control” means the robot continuously adjusts joint positions to maintain upright posture. Sensors detect tilt. Actuators correct it. This happens hundreds of times per second. The draft standard proposes performance thresholds for balance recovery under rated load.
facilities make. AGVs follow fixed paths. Humanoid robots navigate dynamically. Your safety protocols must account for unpredictable routes.
Waiting for ISO 25785-1 to finalize before addressing humanoid robot safety.
The standard is still developing, but the hazards exist now. Apply best practices from the working draft and manufacturer specifications today.
Frequently Asked Questions
What are the safety standards for humanoid robots in 2026?
The primary standards are ISO 10218-1:2025, ISO 10218-2:2025, and ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025. ISO 10218 focuses on collaborative applications rather than hardware alone. The entire workspace must be assessed. ISO 25785-1, currently under development, will specifically address dynamically stable robots including humanoids. Until its publication, facilities should follow manufacturer specifications and ISO 10218 principles. The 2025 revision was substantial: ISO 10218-2:2025 nearly tripled in length, with the safety requirements section growing from 28 to 50 pages, and the update involved experts from more than 20 countries over eight years. For European operations, the EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 applies in parallel from January 2027, and the EU AI Act classifies autonomous robots as high-risk AI systems, with obligations from 2 August 2028 for AI embedded in machinery after the 2026 Digital Omnibus postponed the original deadlines.
Is ISO/TS 15066 still valid for collaborative robots?
How does OSHA regulate walking robots?
OSHA uses the General Duty Clause (Section 5(a)(1)) and references ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025. No specific humanoid standard exists yet. Inspectors verify adherence to consensus standards like ISO 10218 and manufacturer safety specifications. Failure to follow recognized standards can be cited as a recognized hazard. The financial risk is concrete: one Midwest manufacturer with no documented energy control procedures was fined $15,400 per robot, totaling $107,800 across seven robots. □ 동 사업은 서비스로봇 분야의 표준 선점, 서비스로봇 기업을 위한 실증테스트 환경 제공 등을 중심으로 한 문제/이슈는 적절하게 발굴되었으나, 사업추진을 위한 내용 제시가 미흡함
○ 제조업용 로봇 대비 서비스로봇의 낮은 비중, 산업용 로봇과의 차별성 미흡 추세 등을 고려할 때, 기획 단계에서 수요조사와 기존 시설 현황 분석 등을 통해 인프라의 구성, 규모 등이 분석 결정되어야 하나, 이에 관한 내용이 반영되지 않음
○ 주관부처에서 구축하고자 하는 실내외 실환경 테스트필드는 서비스로봇의 실증을 위해 활용될 것이므로 상용화될 서비스로봇이 실제 사용되는 환경과 유사해야 함에도 이에 관한 내용이 기획보고서와 소명자료를 통하여 제시하지 않음
○ 주관부처는 로봇 관련 기존 시설과 구축 예정 시설2)에 대한 현황 파악을 바탕으로 차별성을 제시하고, 사업종료 후에도 자립이 가능할 수 있는 구체적 운영계획 제시가 필요함
□ 인프라 항목과 규모는 서비스로봇의 시장 규모, 기업 니즈 등을 바탕으로 구성될 필요가 있음
○ 제조업용 로봇 대비 서비스로봇의 낮은 비중, 산업용 로봇과의 차별성 미흡 추세, 서비스로봇의 다양성 등을 고려하여 공통으로 필요한 항목, 개별 서비스로봇에만 필요한 항목 등으로 구분한 후, 우선순위를 바탕으로 구성할 필요가 있음
